what_its_for: Thiamine is a B vitamin that your body needs to turn food into energy. It is used to prevent or treat low thiamine levels (thiamine deficiency). It may also be used for certain nerve or heart problems caused by low thiamine, including a serious condition called Wernicke's encephalopathy (a brain disorder often seen in people who drink too much alcohol or have poor nutrition).
how_to_take: Take thiamine tablets by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you have trouble swallowing tablets, ask your pharmacist if a liquid form is available. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. If you are receiving thiamine as a shot or IV, a healthcare provider will give it to you in a clinic or hospital.
dosing: The dose your doctor prescribes will depend on your age, health condition, and the reason you are taking thiamine. For adults treating a deficiency, doses typically range from 5 mg to 100 mg taken one to three times daily. For prevention, lower doses are usually used. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's exact instructions and do not take more or less than prescribed without asking your healthcare provider first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store thiamine tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use thiamine after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol while taking thiamine, as alcohol can block your body from absorbing and using thiamine properly. Also avoid taking antacids at the same time as thiamine, as they may reduce how well it is absorbed — try to space them apart by at least 2 hours. Do not take more than the recommended dose unless your doctor tells you to.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience any signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as hives, difficulty breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat. Also contact your doctor if you notice any skin rash, itching, or redness; feel dizzy or lightheaded; experience nausea or vomiting that does not go away; or if your symptoms do not improve after taking thiamine as directed. If you receive thiamine by injection, tell your provider immediately if you notice pain, swelling, or redness at the injection site.
when_it_works: Many people begin to feel better within a few days to a couple of weeks after starting thiamine, especially if their symptoms were caused by a deficiency. Nerve-related symptoms may take several weeks or months to fully improve. Some damage caused by very low thiamine levels may take a long time to heal or may not fully recover. Continue taking thiamine for as long as your doctor recommends, even if you start to feel better.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Thiamine is generally considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding when taken at recommended doses, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or nursing. Children: Thiamine can be used in children at doses determined by their doctor. Older adults: Older adults may be at higher risk for thiamine deficiency and should follow their doctor's dosing guidance. People with kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions before starting thiamine. People who drink alcohol heavily: You may need higher doses of thiamine, and your doctor should monitor your levels closely.
